root_cause.text: The QRTR nameservice (ns) lacked a per-node limit on the number of server registrations, allowing an unprivileged client to send an unbounded number of NEW_SERVER messages, consume memory, and potentially exhaust system resources.
root_cause.evidence: The commit message states "Current code does no bound checking on the number of servers added per node. A malicious client can flood NEW_SERVER messages and exhaust memory." The patch introduces a per-node counter (`node->server_count`) and a hard limit (`QRTR_NS_MAX_SERVERS = 256`), rejecting new server additions when the limit is exceeded.

A malicious client can flood NEW_SERVER messages and exhaust memory." candidates.rationale: The node structure lacks a field to track the number of servers or enforce a limit, allowing unlimited server registrations per node.
Allocates a new server entry without checking any per-node limit, enabling unbounded memory consumption by successive NEW_SERVER messages.
Stores the server into the node's xarray without any capacity check, directly allowing an unlimited number of server registrations.
Retrieves (or implicitly creates) the node; if the node is new it also has no limit, contributing to the ability to register many servers.
Sets the port for the server being registered; part of the registration sequence that occurs without any limit check.

vuln_statements.explanation: This statement allocates memory for a new server entry without any per-node limit check, enabling an unprivileged client to send unbounded NEW_SERVER messages and exhaust system memory.
This statement stores the newly allocated server into the node's servers xarray without any capacity check, directly allowing unlimited server registrations per node and resource exhaustion.

This field definition lacks any accompanying per-node limit (e.g., a maximum counter or bound), meaning there is no mechanism to cap the number of servers registered on a node, enabling unbounded growth.

This statement retrieves or creates a node structure without imposing any limit on the number of servers that can be associated with that node, contributing to the ability to register an arbitrary number of servers.

This statement sets the port for the server being registered; while not directly causing resource exhaustion, it is an essential step in the registration sequence that occurs without any per-node limit check, making the vulnerability exploitable.
